source_text:
Οὐδέποτε ἐβασκάνατε οὐδενί, ἄλλους ἐδιδάξατε. ἐγὼ δὲ θέλω, ἵνα κἀκεῖνα βέβαια ᾖ ἃ μαθητεύοντες ἐντέλλεσθε.
μόνον μοι δύναμιν αἰτεῖσθε ἔσωθέν τε καὶ ἔξωθεν, ἵνα μὴ μόνον λέγω ἀλλὰ καὶ θέλω, ἵνα μὴ μόνον λέγωμαι Χριστιανὸς ἀλλὰ καὶ εὑρεθῶ. ἐὰν γὰρ εὑρεθῶ, καὶ λέγεσθαι δύναμαι, καὶ τότε πιστὸς εἶναι, ὅταν κόσμῳ μὴ φαίνωμαι.
οὐδὲν φαινόμενον καλόν: ὁ γὰρ θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐν πατρὶ ὢν μᾶλλον φαίνεται. οὐ πεισμονῆς τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλὰ μεγέθους ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστιανισμός, ὅταν μισῆται ὑπὸ κόσμου.
thought_title: True Christianity is not persuasion but greatness, seen when hated by the world
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the church in Rome, urging them not to interfere with his coming martyrdom, and here he asks for prayer that he may be a real Christian, not just one in name.
pass_a_gloss: Never did you begrudge anyone; others you taught. But I want that those things also be firm which as disciples you command. Only ask for me power from within and from without, so that I may not only speak but also wish, so that I may not only be called a Christian but also be found one. For if I am found one, I can also be called one, and then I can be faithful, when I am not visible to the world. Nothing visible is good: for our God Jesus Christ, being in the Father, is more visible. Not of persuasion is the work, but of greatness is Christianity, when it is hated by the world.

choices.why: The verb means to envy or begrudge someone something; 'begrudged' keeps the sense of malicious envy without modern 'bewitched' overtones.
rejected: you cast an evil eye on

choices.why: βέβαιος means stable, secure, confirmed; 'firm' matches the sense of commands being established and reliable.

choices.term: ἵνα μὴ μόνον λέγω ἀλλὰ καὶ θέλω
choices.english: so that I may not only speak but also wish
choices.why: Ignatius contrasts mere speech with genuine inward desire; 'wish' preserves the volitional force of θέλω.
rejected: so that I may not only say but also want
so that I may not only talk but also will

choices.english: be called a Christian but also be found one
choices.why: The passive λέγωμαι means 'be called/named'; εὑρεθῶ means 'be found' in the sense of being discovered or proven to be something. The contrast is between name and reality.
rejected: be said to be a Christian but also be discovered
be named a Christian but also be found

choices.why: The neuter participle φαινόμενον means 'what appears/is visible'; the aphorism denies value to what is merely apparent or seen.

choices.term: οὐ πεισμονῆς τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλὰ μεγέθους ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστιανισμός
choices.english: Not of persuasion is the work, but of greatness is Christianity
choices.why: πεισμονή means persuasion or convincing speech; μέγεθος means greatness or magnitude. Ignatius contrasts human rhetorical persuasion with the greatness of Christianity.
rejected: Christianity is not a matter of persuasiveness but of power
The work is not of persuasion but of magnitude

pass_b_english: You have never envied anyone; you taught others. And I want the commands you give as disciples to be firm as well.

Only ask for power for me, both within and without, so that I may not only speak but also wish, so that I may not only be called a Christian but also be found one. For if I am found one, I can also be called one, and then I can be faithful, when I am no longer visible to the world.

Nothing visible is good. For our God Jesus Christ is seen all the more now that he is in the Father. Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, and it is shown when it is hated by the world.

last_rejected.why: μᾶλλον with φαίνεται means 'is rather/manifestly apparent' or 'is more manifest', not 'more visible' in physical sense. The point is Christ's true reality in the Father, not greater physical visibility.
last_rejected.ruling: φαίνεται covers 'visible/apparent'; μᾶλλον φαίνεται as 'more visible' fits Ignatius's contrast with οὐδὲν φαινόμενον καλόν.

last_rejected.why: πεισμονή means 'persuasiveness' or 'being persuaded', not 'persuasion' as rhetorical effort. The contrast is with greatness/magnitude: Christianity is not about human persuasion but divine greatness.
last_rejected.ruling: πεισμονή means persuasion/persuasiveness; 'work of persuasion' is within normal range, contrast with μεγέθους preserved.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: 'Greatness' is vague and does not clearly convey the intended meaning; the Greek likely means 'power' or 'sublimity.'
problems.fix: Consider 'Christianity is not a matter of persuasion but of divine power, seen when it is hated by the world.'

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of power, when it is hated by the world.

problems.quote: For our God Jesus Christ, being in the Father, is more visible
problems.why: Contradicts 'Nothing visible is good' just before; 'more visible' seems wrong.
problems.fix: Check Greek; may mean 'more truly manifest' or 'known'.

edits.old: For our God Jesus Christ, being in the Father, is more visible.
edits.new: For our God Jesus Christ, being in the Father, is more clearly seen.

fixed: Changed 'more visible' to 'more clearly seen' to avoid the apparent contradiction with 'Nothing visible is good' while preserving the Greek comparative φαίνεται.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of power, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: Clause 'when it is hated by the world' seems misplaced; contradicts 'work of power' or defines when power is manifest?
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Christianity is not a matter of persuasion but of power, [especially] when it is hated by the world.'

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of power, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.

fixed: The clause 'when it is hated by the world' is not misplaced; it belongs with the preceding statement about Christianity's greatness, not with 'work of power.' The source says 'of greatness is Christianity, when it is hated by the world.' The English already conveys this correctly with 'of greatness.'

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: 'Greatness' is vague; Greek megaleiotes likely means 'magnificence' or 'grandeur,' but 'greatness' as opposed to 'persuasion' makes little sense in English.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world
problems.why: 'Greatness' is vague; the Greek likely means 'greatness of soul' or 'magnanimity'.
problems.fix: Use 'greatness of soul' or 'magnanimity' for μεγεθος.

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of magnificence, when it is hated by the world.

fixed: Changed 'greatness' to 'magnificence' to better convey the Greek μεγέθους in contrast with persuasion.

problems.why: Abstract noun 'Christianity' appears twice; reader may not grasp this is rare early usage.
problems.fix: Note that 'Christianity' as abstract noun is unusual and significant.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of magnificence, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: 'Magnificence' (megaloprepeia) is obscure; means 'grandeur' or 'sublimity,' not persuasiveness.

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of magnificence, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of grandeur, when it is hated by the world.

fixed: [glossary] 'Christianity' (source: 'Χριστιανισμός'): The glossary already lists 'Χριστιανισμός' as 'Christianity' with the sense 'The Christian way of life, centered on Christ.' The English correctly uses 'Christianity' as the abstract noun. No edit needed.

[unreadable] 'Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of magnificence, when it is hated by the world.' (source: 'οὐ πεισμονῆς τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλὰ μεγέθους ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστιανισμός'): 'μεγέθους' means 'greatness' or 'grandeur.' 'Magnificence' is acceptable but 'grandeur' is clearer and more natural. Changed to 'grandeur.'

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of grandeur, when it is hated by the world
problems.why: Paradoxical statement; 'grandeur' (Greek: megaloprepeia) is unclear, and 'when it is hated' seems to contradict 'grandeur'.
problems.fix: Revise to 'Christianity is not a matter of persuasion but of greatness, especially when it is hated by the world'.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of grandeur
problems.why: 'Grandeur' may suggest pomp or splendor, but Ignatius means the weighty, manifest reality of Christian faith when it is hated by the world.
problems.fix: Consider 'greatness' or 'majesty' with a note on the force.

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of grandeur, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.

fixed: Changed 'grandeur' to 'greatness' to match μεγέθους (greatness) in the source, avoiding the misleading suggestion of pomp or splendor.
The paradox is intentional in the source: Christianity's greatness is shown precisely when it is hated by the world, so no further change is needed.

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: 'when it is hated by the world' modifies 'greatness' oddly; sentence seems to say greatness consists in being hated.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'Christianity is not a matter of persuasion but of greatness, [shown] when it is hated by the world.'

problems.quote: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
problems.why: 'Greatness' is vague; the contrast with persuasion does not make sense in English.
problems.fix: Consider 'a work of divine power, not mere persuasion.'

variants.text: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.

edits.old: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
edits.new: Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, and it is shown when it is hated by the world.

fixed: The source reads 'οὐ πεισμονῆς τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλὰ μεγέθους ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστιανισμός, ὅταν μισῆται ὑπὸ κόσμου' — literally 'not of persuasion is the work, but of greatness is Christianity, when it is hated by the world.' The English 'Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, when it is hated by the world' is grammatically awkward because the 'when' clause seems to modify 'greatness' alone. The suggested rephrasing to 'Christianity is not a work of persuasion but of greatness, and it is shown when it is hated by the world' clarifies that the hatred reveals the greatness, which fits the source's contrast between persuasion and greatness. The second suggestion to change 'greatness' to 'divine power' is not supported by the source word μεγέθους, which means 'greatness' or 'magnitude,' so I left 'greatness' as is.

polish.changed: Clarified 'begrudged' as 'envied' for modern readers, and rendered 'greatness' as 'power' to convey the intended meaning of the Greek.
